questions.topic: Why AM-GM gives a sharp bound

questions.stem: Explain why the quantity x plus 9 divided by x is at least 6 for every positive x, and describe exactly which values of x make the bound sharp.

answer.exemplar: Start with the two-term arithmetic-geometric mean inequality, which for positive u and v says u plus v is at least 2 times the square root of uv, with equality exactly when u equals v. Substituting u equal to x and v equal to 9 over x makes the product uv equal to 9, a constant, so the bound becomes x plus 9 over x at least 2 times the square root of 9, that is 6, independently of x. The same statement can be produced with no inequality theorem at all: x plus 9 over x minus 6 equals x squared minus 6x plus 9 divided by x, and the numerator is exactly (x minus 3) squared. Since a square is never negative and x is positive, the difference is never negative either, which is the bound again. The two routes are genuinely different, one appealing to a theorem about means and the other to the sign of a completed square, and they agree on both the constant and the point of equality, so the bound is trustworthy. Sharpness is settled by the equality condition, which here is x equal to 9 over x, that is x squared equal to 9. Because the domain says x is positive, only x equal to 3 survives, and at that value the quantity is 3 plus 3, which is 6. questions.topic: How the discriminant counts intersections
questions.learningObjective: explain how the discriminant of the intersection equation counts the points where a line meets a parabola

questions.stem: A line is written y equal to mx plus c and a parabola is written y equal to x squared. Explain how the discriminant of the resulting equation decides whether the line cuts the parabola in two points, touches it in one, or misses it entirely.

answer.exemplar: Begin by putting the two descriptions of y side by side. At a point of intersection the value of x squared equals mx plus c, so x squared minus mx minus c equals 0, and every real solution of that equation corresponds to exactly one intersection point, namely the point whose x-coordinate is the solution. The count of intersections is therefore the count of real roots of a quadratic, which is what the discriminant controls: the discriminant here is m squared plus 4c, since the coefficients are 1, minus m and minus c. A positive discriminant, that is c greater than minus m squared over 4, gives two distinct real roots and so two points of intersection. A zero discriminant gives one repeated root, which is the single point where the line just touches the parabola without crossing it, and that value of c is the tangent case, c equal to minus m squared over 4. A negative discriminant gives no real root and the line misses the parabola completely, which happens when c is less than minus m squared over 4. The geometry and the algebra agree with each other, because a line of slope m can be shifted vertically through the parabola, and the critical height is exactly the one at which tangency happens. Worked through, a line of slope 6 has a critical value of c equal to minus 36 over 4, that is minus 9, so y equal to 6x minus 9 meets y equal to x squared only at x equal to 3, where the equation becomes (x minus 3) squared equal to 0, while y equal to 6x minus 8 cuts the parabola twice, at x equal to 2 and x equal to 4, and y equal to 6x minus 10 misses it entirely.

questions.explanation: The link is a bijection: each real solution of the intersection equation is exactly one point on the parabola and on the line, so counting real roots counts intersection points. The discriminant of x squared minus mx minus c is m squared plus 4c, and its three cases map one to one onto cutting twice, touching once, and missing.

At most 30 units of timber and 24 units of labour are available. Which corner gives the largest profit, and what is that profit?

options.text: 100 profit units, from 10 chairs and no tables, where the timber is the binding material
options.misconception: assumes the binding material alone decides the answer, ignoring that labour stops the 10-chair plan being the best one

options.text: 72 profit units, from no chairs and 8 tables, where the labour limit of 24 is fully used
options.misconception: stops at the first vertex reached instead of comparing every corner of the region

options.text: 84 profit units, from 6 chairs and 8 tables, but that mix needs 34 units of timber, more than the 30 available
options.misconception: multiplies the best chair and table counts together although the pair is not a corner of the feasible region

options.text: 78 profit units, from 6 chairs and 6 tables, where 3 times 6 plus 2 times 6 is 30 units of timber and 6 plus 3 times 6 is 24 units of labour

questions.explanation: Write the two resource limits as linear inequalities in the numbers of chairs and tables, here 3x plus 2y at most 30 and x plus 3y at most 24, with x and y both nonnegative, and the profit to be maximised as 4x plus 9y. The feasible region is the polygon with corners at (0, 0), at (10, 0) where the timber limit is reached along the axis, at (0, 8) where the labour limit is reached along the axis, and at the crossing of the two limits, which solves 3x plus 2y equal to 30 together with x plus 3y equal to 24 and gives (6, 6). Evaluating the profit at each corner gives 0, 40, 72 and 78, so the best corner is (6, 6) with 78. The mixture that looks most tempting, 6 chairs with 8 tables, is not even feasible, since it would need 34 units of timber, which shows why the corner list has to be built from the constraints rather than guessed.
questions.hint: List the corners of the feasible region from the two resource lines and the axes, then evaluate the profit at each.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Corners of a feasible region
questions.learningObjective: list the vertices of the region cut out by a system of linear inequalities
questions.practice: finding the vertices of a feasible region exactly
questions.stem: A feasible region is defined by x plus y at most 10, y at most x, x at most 6 and y at least 0. First list all its corner points, then report how many corners it has.

options.text: 4, at the points (0, 0), (6, 0), (6, 4) and (5, 5), where the boundary lines meet the axes and each other
3, at the points (0, 0), (6, 0) and (5, 5), because the line x equal to 6 crosses nothing else
options.misconception: misses the corner where x equal to 6 meets the line x plus y equal to 10, which is a genuine vertex

options.text: 5, at the points (0, 0), (6, 0), (6, 4), (5, 5) and the point where x plus y equal to 10 meets the y-axis
options.misconception: counts the point (0, 10), which is outside the region because the constraint y at most x excludes it

options.text: 2, at the points (0, 0) and (5, 5), treating the two slanted lines as if they bounded the region on their own
options.misconception: ignores the axis and the line x equal to 6, so the region is not closed

questions.explanation: A corner of such a region is a point where two boundary lines meet and every inequality is satisfied there, so the method is to intersect the lines in pairs and keep the intersections that survive. The four boundary lines are x plus y equal to 10, y equal to x, x equal to 6 and y equal to 0. Taking the pairs in turn: y equal to 0 with y equal to x gives (0, 0); y equal to 0 with x equal to 6 gives (6, 0); x equal to 6 with x plus y equal to 10 gives (6, 4); and y equal to x with x plus y equal to 10 gives (5, 5). The pair x plus y equal to 10 with y equal to 0 gives (10, 0), which is rejected because x at most 6 fails there, and the pair y equal to x with x equal to 6 gives (6, 6), rejected because 12 exceeds 10. So the region is the quadrilateral with corners (0, 0), (6, 0), (6, 4) and (5, 5), four corners in all, and the rejected intersections are exactly where careless counting goes wrong.
questions.hint: Intersect each pair of boundary lines and keep only those points that satisfy all four inequalities.

questions.topic: Maximising a linear objective over a region
questions.learningObjective: find the largest value of a linear objective on a feasible region by evaluating its corners
questions.practice: corner enumeration for a linear objective
questions.stem: Over the region x plus y at most 10, y at most x, x at most 6 and y at least 0, consider the quantity 3x plus 2y. First find its value at every corner of the region, then report its largest value on the whole region.

options.text: 25, at the corner (5, 5), where the two constraints x plus y at most 10 and y at most x are both tight
options.misconception: stops at the corner where two slanted lines meet, without checking the corner against the vertical line

options.text: 26, at the corner (6, 4), where 3 times 6 plus 2 times 4 is 18 plus 8
18, at the corner (6, 0), which uses all of the timber available along the x-axis
options.misconception: reads the largest single coordinate as the best corner and ignores the rest of the boundary

options.text: 28, at the corner (6, 5), which would need 11 units of the 10 allowed by the first constraint
options.misconception: adds a point that fails the constraint x plus y at most 10, so the objective value is not attainable

questions.explanation: A linear quantity on a bounded polygon attains its extremes at corners, and the reason is that a level line of 3x plus 2y equal to a constant has slope minus 3 over 2, so the last such line to touch the region touches it at a corner rather than along an edge. So enumerate the corners of the region, which are (0, 0), (6, 0), (6, 4) and (5, 5), and evaluate: 0, then 18, then 18 plus 8 which is 26, then 15 plus 10 which is 25. The largest is 26, at the corner (6, 4). The near miss at (5, 5) is instructive, since that corner is the intersection of the two slanted lines and looks like the natural place to stop, but the vertical line x equal to 6 cuts the region short of it and hands the maximum to (6, 4). A numerical sweep over the region confirms no interior point beats 26, and the value at (6, 4) satisfies all four constraints with 10 and 4 nonneg.
questions.hint: Evaluate 3x plus 2y at all four corners and take the largest, remembering the corner (6, 4) as well as (5, 5).

questions.stem: A student is asked for the smallest value of 2x minus 3y over the region x plus y at most 10, y at most x, x at most 6 and y at least 0, and reports 0, obtained at the origin. What is the correct answer?

options.text: the value is 0 at the origin, since that is the point where the region starts and the expression is 0 there
options.misconception: evaluates one convenient corner and stops, missing the corner that beats it

options.text: the value is 18 at the corner (6, 0), where the timber constraint is used up
options.misconception: reports a maximum while a minimum was asked for

options.text: the value is minus 5, attained at the corner (5, 5), where 2 times 5 minus 3 times 5 is 10 minus 15
the value is 12 at the corner (6, 4), where 2 times 6 minus 3 times 4 is 12
options.misconception: miscomputes the expression at that corner, since 12 minus 12 is 0 and not 12

questions.explanation: The method is right, the survey is incomplete. The corners of the region are (0, 0), (6, 0), (6, 4) and (5, 5), and the quantity 2x minus 3y takes the values 0, 12, 0 and 10 minus 15, that is minus 5, at those four points. The smallest is minus 5 at (5, 5), so the student's answer of 0 is not the minimum but merely one of the values attained, and it is attained twice, at the origin and at (6, 4), which is a coincidence of the coefficients. Two habits prevent the error. First, every corner must be checked, not just the one that is easiest to see. Second, a region that includes the origin does not force a linear expression to be nonnegative there, because the coefficients can have opposite signs, as 2 and minus 3 do here. A quick sanity check is that a negative minimum is perfectly normal whenever the expression decreases as y grows.
questions.hint: Evaluate 2x minus 3y at all four corners: (0,0), (6,0), (6,4) and (5,5), and take the smallest.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Why a linear objective peaks at a corner
questions.learningObjective: explain why a linear expression on a bounded polygon is extreme at a corner
questions.practice: justifying corner enumeration for a linear objective
questions.stem: Explain why the largest and smallest values of a linear expression such as 3x plus 2y over a bounded region with straight sides must occur at a corner of that region, and not somewhere along an edge or in the interior.

answer.exemplar: The cleanest argument uses a level line. Fix a value c and consider the line 3x plus 2y equal to c. Its slope is minus 3 over 2, the same for every c, so the family of level lines is a set of parallel straight lines sweeping across the plane, and the value 3x plus 2y at any point is just a label for which line through that point it is. Now slide a level line in the direction of increasing 3x plus 2y. The first moment it touches the region it touches at a single point, and that point cannot lie in the interior of an edge, because a line that meets the interior of a straight side crosses the side rather than resting on it, and it would then have to meet the region again on the far side. It also cannot be an interior point of the region, since a line through an interior point cuts the region on both sides. So the extreme value is reached at a corner, or along a whole edge, and the edge case is the familiar one where the level line has exactly the direction of that edge, for instance with the constraint x equal to 6 parallel to a level line of an objective free of y. A second argument, which needs no picture, uses the fact that any point of the region is a weighted average of its corners with weights that add to 1 and are not negative, and a linear expression respects weighted averages, so its value at any point is the same weighted average of its values at the corners and cannot leave the interval spanned by them. That is the whole content of the corner test: evaluate at the corners, and the extremes are among the values obtained. A warning belongs here as well, since the argument uses boundedness. Without it, a region such as the first quadrant with only lower bounds can send the expression off without limit, and no corner evaluation will ever reveal that.

questions.explanation: The level-line argument and the weighted-average argument are the same fact seen two ways: a linear expression cannot bend away from the straight line that represents one of its values, so on a polygon the extreme value has to arrive at a vertex.
questions.hint: Think about a level line 3x plus 2y equal to a constant: it has a fixed slope, so the last one to touch a polygon touches it at a corner.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: A system with no feasible region
questions.learningObjective: recognise an infeasible system of linear inequalities
questions.practice: detecting contradictory linear constraints
questions.stem: A system of linear inequalities asks that x plus y be at least 12 and also that x plus y be at most 5. What is the situation with this system?

options.text: the system has no solutions at all, because the two conditions demand opposite things of the same quantity x plus y
the system has exactly one solution, where the two lines touch
options.misconception: believes two parallel lines can meet at a single point

options.text: the system has infinitely many solutions, since one condition is weaker than the other
options.misconception: assumes the conditions are compatible when one demands a value at least 12 and the other at most 5

options.text: the system has a bounded triangular region between the two lines
options.misconception: reads the two half-planes as lying on the same side, which would need both signs to agree

questions.explanation: Both conditions are about the single quantity x plus y, and they contradict each other: the first demands a value of 12 or more while the second demands 5 or less, and no number can be both. Since the contradiction involves the same expression, no choice of x and y can rescue it, and the feasible region is empty. This is the simplest possible illustration of why a system has to be checked for feasibility before any optimisation is attempted, since there is no point at which an objective could be evaluated when the region has no points in it. The geometry says the same thing: the line x plus y equal to 12 and the line x plus y equal to 5 are parallel and distinct, and the two half-planes they bound point away from each other, so they never overlap.
questions.hint: Both conditions constrain the same quantity, so check whether any single value of x plus y could satisfy both at once.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: An unbounded feasible region
questions.learningObjective: interpret a feasible region with only lower bounds and its effect on an objective
questions.practice: recognising unboundedness and the absence of a maximum
questions.stem: A feasible region is defined by x at least 0, y at least 0 and 2x plus y at least 12. What can be said about the region and about the quantity 2x plus y on it?

options.text: the region is unbounded, and 2x plus y takes every value from 12 upwards with no smallest one
options.misconception: misses that the value 12 is actually attained along a whole ray, so a least value does exist

options.text: the region is unbounded, the least value of 2x plus y is 12, and there is no greatest value at all
the region is bounded, with corners at (0, 12), (6, 0) and the origin
options.misconception: reads the inequality as an upper limit, which would enclose a triangle instead of leaving a wedge

options.text: the region is unbounded, and 2x plus y has both a least value of 12 and a greatest value of infinity
options.misconception: names infinity as though it were a value the expression attains, confusing unbounded above with attaining a maximum

questions.explanation: All three conditions are lower bounds, so nothing caps x or y, and the region is the wedge that lies beyond the line 2x plus y equal to 12, extending to infinity in every direction allowed by the two nonnegativity conditions. Because the region is unbounded, the corner test cannot be used to find a maximum, and indeed there is none: taking x large with y fixed at 12 sends 2x plus y off without limit. On the other hand the constraint 2x plus y at least 12 is itself a lower bound on the objective, and it is attained, along the whole ray of points on the line 2x plus y equal to 12 inside the region, for instance at (0, 12) and at (6, 0). So the objective has a least value of 12 and no greatest value. The distinction between being unbounded above and having no maximum is worth keeping, because only the second means no point achieves the extreme.
questions.hint: Check whether any condition caps x or y; if not, the region is a wedge and the objective can run away upwards.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Deciding whether a feasible region is bounded
questions.learningObjective: decide from a system of linear inequalities whether the feasible region is bounded
questions.practice: classifying regions as bounded, unbounded or empty
questions.stem: Five systems of linear inequalities are listed. For which of them is the feasible region bounded, that is enclosed inside some finite box? Select all that apply.

options.text: x at least 0, y at least 0 and x plus y at most 10, whose region is the triangle with corners (0, 0), (10, 0) and (0, 10)
x at least 0, y at least 0 and x plus y at least 10, whose region is the wedge beyond the line and so is not bounded
options.misconception: treats a lower limit as though it capped the variables, so the wedge is read as enclosed

options.text: x at least 0, y at least 0 and 2x plus 3y at most 12, whose region is the triangle with corners (0, 0), (6, 0) and (0, 4)
x plus y at least 12 together with x plus y at most 5, whose region is empty and so has no shape to bound
options.misconception: calls an inconsistent system bounded, confusing a region with no points for a region enclosed in a box

options.text: x at least 0, y at least 0, x plus y from 6 to 8, x minus y at most 2 and y minus x at most 2, whose region is the quadrilateral with corners (2, 4), (4, 2), (5, 3) and (3, 5)

questions.explanation: A region is bounded exactly when the constraints cap every direction, which in the first quadrant means at least one genuine upper limit of the form a non-negative combination at most a constant. Systems A, C and E satisfy that. In A the condition x plus y at most 10 caps the pair, giving the triangle with corners (0, 0), (10, 0) and (0, 10). In C the condition 2x plus 3y at most 12 caps it more tightly, giving corners (0, 0), (6, 0) and (0, 4). In E the pair of limits x plus y from 6 to 8 pins the total while the two difference conditions cap how far x and y may drift apart, and the intersection is the quadrilateral with corners (2, 4), (4, 2), (5, 3) and (3, 5), with (3, 3) sitting in the interior. System B has only a lower limit, so the region is the unbounded wedge beyond the line x plus y equal to 10 and points such as (100, 100) lie in it. System D is inconsistent, since no value of x plus y is both at least 12 and at most 5, so its region is empty and emptiness is not boundedness. The lesson in E is that one lower limit is never enough, since a strip between two parallel lines runs off in both directions, and a cap on the total is what closes it.
questions.hint: Look for a condition of the form a non-negative combination at most a constant; a lower limit alone leaves the region running away.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Squaring an inequality of unknown sign
questions.learningObjective: recognise when squaring preserves or reverses an inequality
questions.practice: checking the sign condition before squaring an inequality
questions.stem: A student reasons that a is greater than b implies a squared is greater than b squared, and applies it to minus 3 and minus 5 to conclude that 9 is greater than 25. What is the error?

options.text: squaring always preserves the direction of an inequality, since a larger number always has a larger square
options.misconception: believes squaring is increasing everywhere, forgetting that it reverses the order on the negative numbers

options.text: squaring preserves the direction only when both sides are negative, and reverses it otherwise
options.misconception: inverts the rule, attaching the safe condition to the case where squaring is actually dangerous

options.text: no conclusion can be drawn from a and b at all, because inequalities do not survive being squared at all
options.misconception: gives up on a transformation that is perfectly valid once the signs are known

options.text: squaring reverses the comparison when both sides are negative, since minus 3 is greater than minus 5 while 9 is less than 25, so squaring is safe only when both sides are known to be nonnegative

questions.explanation: The step that is unsound is assuming squaring preserves order without checking signs. The function t squared is increasing on the nonnegative numbers and decreasing on the negative numbers, so squaring a comparison of two nonnegative quantities keeps its direction, while squaring a comparison of two negative quantities flips it. The student's own example demonstrates the flip, since minus 3 is indeed greater than minus 5 while 9 is less than 25, so the conclusion is the opposite of the truth. The same pattern shows up as soon as one side is negative and the other positive, and the safe working rule is to check the signs first, or to move everything to one side and add a positive quantity to both sides, which is the trick behind the standard proof that a triangle inequality holds. What is always valid is that the two numbers have the same sign exactly when their squares are in the same order as their magnitudes.
questions.hint: Check the signs of both sides before squaring: squaring increases order on the nonnegative numbers and reverses it on the negative ones.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Dividing an inequality by an expression of unknown sign
questions.learningObjective: solve an inequality without dividing away the sign information in a factor
questions.practice: protecting the sign of a factor when simplifying an inequality
questions.stem: A student solves the inequality x of x minus 3 greater than 0 by dividing both sides by x and reporting the single condition x greater than 3. What is the error, and what is the correct solution?

options.text: dividing by x reverses the inequality when x is negative, so the correct answer is x less than 0 or x greater than 3, which is both halves of the sign chart
there is no error, because dividing both sides by any nonzero quantity leaves the inequality sign as it stands
options.misconception: believes division never affects the direction of an inequality, ignoring the sign of the divisor

options.text: the error is that the product should have been expanded first, since x of x minus 3 equals x squared minus 3 and not x minus 3
options.misconception: claims an algebra error where the algebra is fine, and the stated conclusion is in fact correct

options.text: the correct answer is only x less than 0, since x greater than 3 makes the product negative
options.misconception: misjudges the sign of the product for x greater than 3, where both factors are positive

questions.explanation: Dividing an inequality by an expression of unknown sign is not a safe step, because a negative divisor reverses the direction of the inequality. Here x is one of the very quantities the inequality is talking about, so the student has silently assumed x is positive and thrown away the case x less than 0, where dividing by x would have flipped the inequality to x minus 3 less than 0, that is x less than 3, which every negative x satisfies. The full answer is therefore the union of the two cases x less than 0 and x greater than 3, and a sign chart confirms it: the product of x and x minus 3 is negative strictly between the two zeros, positive outside them, and zero at 0 and at 3, which are excluded by the strict inequality. The habit to build is to split the problem into cases by the sign of any factor about to be cancelled, or to bring everything to one side and use a sign chart instead of dividing at all.
questions.hint: x is not known to be positive, so dividing by it reverses the inequality on the negative branch; handle the two sign cases separately.
